name: Hallucination Risks in Clinical Content
blurb: Why generative AI output needs verification in trials.
title: Hallucination Risks in Clinical Content
answer: General purpose language models can produce convincing but false clinical content. Researchers showed a model could fabricate a plausible clinical trial dataset in minutes, and studies of generated references found large shares invented or inaccurate. In trial documents every claim must trace to source data.

reading.body:
General purpose language models can fabricate convincing clinical content, so no generated claim in a trial document should be accepted without a trace to source data.

Two documented results establish the pattern. A model produced a fake but plausible clinical trial dataset in minutes. Separately, 47 percent of references it generated were fabricated and another 46 percent were inaccurate, meaning roughly nine in ten were unusable as citations.

Trial documents are held to a different standard than drafts. Every claim must trace to source data, so a fabricated reference is not a stylistic flaw but a defect that invalidates the document it appears in. The recommended control follows from that: retrieval tied to the team's own documents, with citations to source records, and no unsourced generated facts accepted.

The data covers two 2023 findings and a verification practice. It does not measure how often these failures reach submitted trial documents, does not compare models, and does not address whether retrieval eliminates fabrication rather than reducing it.

explainer:
Generative language models produce fluent text by predicting likely words, not by checking facts. When they lack information they can fill gaps with plausible inventions, known as hallucinations: citations that do not exist, numbers that were never measured, or confident summaries that misstate a study. Researchers have shown models can fabricate entire realistic looking datasets on request.

In clinical development this is a serious risk, because documents and analyses feed regulatory and medical decisions. The defences are well understood: ground generation in retrieved source documents, require citations that point to specific records, constrain models to drafting and summarising rather than computing results, verify every number against validated outputs, and keep qualified reviewers accountable. Data integrity controls also matter, since fabricated data must be distinguishable from real data by design.

Why hallucination is dangerous in clinical content

A language model produces fluent text whether or not it has a source. In clinical documents that fluency hides the error: a dose that is slightly wrong, an adverse event attributed to the wrong drug, a trial result stated with the wrong direction of effect, or an eligibility criterion that was never in the protocol. Each reads naturally and passes a casual review. In a protocol, a consent form, a safety narrative or a study report, such an error can reach a patient or a regulator.

Where it shows up

The risk is highest when a model is asked for specifics it was not given: exact values, references, and details of a particular trial. It is lower when the model is restricted to rewriting or summarising text that is supplied to it, and lower again when the output is checked against structured data. Patient facing material carries its own risk: a model simplifying a consent form can remove a nuance that changes what the patient is agreeing to.

What clinical teams do about it

The controls are consistent across the industry. Use retrieval so the model works only from supplied, verified sources. Require citations to those sources for every factual statement. Check every number automatically against the data it came from. Keep clinicians and medical writers reviewing and owning content, with machine written sections marked so review attention goes where it is needed. And train people to expect confident errors, because the failure mode is not nonsense but plausibility. Companies that measure it report hallucination rates falling sharply with retrieval and verification, but never to zero, which is why the human check stays.
